query: A TiVNbTa refractory high-entropy alloy has been reported in a single-phase BCC, dendritic state, with a yield strength of about 800 MPa and roughly 40% strain under lower-temperature testing, but at 1273 K it retains only 330 MPa yield strength and 423 MPa compressive strength at 30% strain. For its use as an intermediate layer that transfers heat between W and CuCrZr while preserving structural integrity, what single intervention could overcome this loss of strength at elevated temperature? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the reported baseline, define the applicable thermal and mechanical boundary conditions, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a controlled amount of oxygen to induce the formation of fine TiO precipitates in the TiVNbTa alloy will improve its retention of high‐temperature strength by impeding dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: TiVNbTa refractory high-entropy alloy processed by vacuum arc melting and heat treated to yield a single-phase, dendritic BCC microstructure with relatively coarse grains.
generation.intervention: Introduce a deliberate, low-level oxygen addition during processing (or via a controlled post‐processing treatment) to promote the formation of uniformly dispersed nanometric TiO precipitates within the BCC matrix.
generation.conditions: The enhanced alloy is intended for use as an intermediate layer in heat transfer between tungsten and CuCrZr. Its mechanical performance is evaluated under high-temperature conditions (around 1273 K) with typical compressive/tensile loading relevant to structural integrity in thermal barrier applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-scale TiO particles precipitated within the BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The oxide precipitates will provide precipitation strengthening by obstructing dislocation motion and reducing grain boundary sliding at elevated temperatures. This microstructural reinforcement is expected to slow the softening process that normally occurs as temperature increases.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline—where the alloy retains only about 330 MPa yield strength at 1273 K—the oxygen-doped alloy is predicted to show a significantly higher yield strength at these temperatures, thereby better preserving its structural integrity during high-temperature operation. (The exact magnitude of improvement is uncertain but should be noticeably higher than the original 330 MPa.)
generation.baseline: Reported yield strength of approximately 800 MPa at lower temperatures but only about 330 MPa at 1273 K, with ~423 MPa compressive strength at 30% strain.
generation.boundary: The intervention is designed to be effective under elevated temperature conditions (around 1273 K) and mechanical loadings typical of heat transfer interfaces between high-melting point tungsten and CuCrZr heat sink alloys.
generation.uncertainty: The precise increase in strength retention and the long-term stability of the TiO precipitates under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of TiVNbTa alloys: one processed conventionally (without additional oxygen) and one processed with controlled oxygen doping intended to form TiO precipitates. Subject both sets to identical homogenization heat treatments and then perform high-temperature mechanical tests (tensile and compression) at 1273 K. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify the presence and uniformity of TiO precipitates in the oxygen-doped sample.
measurements: Yield strength and compressive strength at 1273 K
Microstructural characterization (TEM/SEM) to confirm precipitate formation
Comparative fractography to assess failure modes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the oxygen-doped alloy fails to show a statistically significant improvement (beyond experimental uncertainty) in high-temperature yield strength or if TEM/SEM analyses do not confirm the formation of a substantial population of fine TiO precipitates compared to the undoped control.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHerein, a TiVNb medium-entropy alloy was prepared via vacuum arc melting. The alloy maintained a body-centred cubic (BCC)-dominant phase following an annealing treatment at 1300 °C for 12 h. Although its structure was coarsened due to grain growth during annealing, the alloy developed a few Ti-rich nanobands and showed an increase in dislocations, resulting in its hardness increasing from 241.7 to 341.1 HV and strength increasing by tens of MPa relative to that of the as-melt TiVNb alloy. The tensile strength of the coarsened alloy reached 647 MPa at room temperature and 405 MPa at 800 °C. Further, the compressive yield strength reached 438 MPa at 800 °C, under which condition the alloy exhibited fewer cracks. Rapid softening was observed at 1200 °C, reducing the yield strength to ∼50 MPa. The coarsened TiVNb alloy showed weak dependence of its strength on temperature.Keywords: TiVNb, Homogenisation, Grain coarsening, Cracking resistance

Equiatomic NbMoTaWVTi refractory HEA has been successfully synthesized by MA and SPS. It exhibits excellent mechanical properties with compressive yield strength of 2709 MPa, fracture strength of 3115 MPa and fracture strain of 11.4%. The sintered alloy consists of a BCC matrix phase, a minor BCC phase, and an FCC precipitated phase, identified as TiO. The average grain size of BCC matrix phase and TiO are measured to be 1.35 μm and 0.46 μm, respectively. Compared with the as-cast NbMoTaWVTi alloy, the compressive yield strength and fracture strength of the alloy in this work are extraordinarily elevated, while the ductility is slightly reduced. Thus, mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering is a promising way to further improve mechanical properties of the refractory HEA by means of grain refinement and precipitation strengthening.
